kernelIdea: ℂ = {a + bi | a,b ∈ ℝ} with i² = −1. Re(z) = a and Im(z) = b are both real. ℝ ⊆ ℂ via a = a + 0i, completing the tower ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ.

kernels.l1: A complex number is two instructions: go across, then turn.
kernels.l2: A complex number is a pair of instructions — how far across, and how far up. Every ordinary number is one of these with no up at all.
kernels.l3: A complex number is written a + bi, where a and b are ordinary numbers and i is the new number with i × i = −1. Every ordinary number is a complex number with b = 0.
kernels.l4: A complex number is an across part plus a turn part, written a + bi, where i multiplied by itself gives −1. Both parts are ordinary real numbers, and the reals sit inside the complex numbers as the ones whose turn part is zero.
kernels.l5: A complex number is fixed by its across part and its turn part, both ordinary reals. The reals sit inside the complex numbers as the ones with no turn.
kernels.l6: A complex number is a pair of reals with a multiplication attached. The across and turn parts are ordinary real numbers, and no ordering of the complex numbers can be compatible with their arithmetic.
kernels.l7: A complex number is an across part plus a turn part, both real, with the turn unit squaring to −1. The reals embed as the numbers with no turn, and no ordering of the complex numbers is compatible with their arithmetic.
kernels.l8: ℂ is ℝ[x]/(x² + 1), a two-dimensional real algebra; the tower ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ is a chain of canonical embeddings, each fixing a defect of the previous system.

kernel: ℂ = {a + bi | a,b ∈ ℝ} with i² = −1. Re(z) = a, Im(z) = b, and both are real. ℝ ⊆ ℂ via a = a + 0i, giving ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ ⊆ ℂ.
